findings.where: Screen 7 (Lean it flat), SHOW text and its read
findings.what: 'At 0 the grid lies flat: no point lands on (3, 2), but every point with x + y = 2 lands on (4, 2).' puts three ideas behind a colon in 23 words, and the second dot at (4, 2) appears without being introduced; split it, e.g. 'At 0 the grid lies flat on one line. No point lands on (3, 2). A second dot at (4, 2) sits on that line. Every point with x + y = 2 lands on it.'

'That matrix times A gives [2 0; 0 2], which is 2 times I, and 2 is A's determinant.' chains three clauses; split it into 'That matrix times A gives [2 0; 0 2]. That is 2 times I. And 2 is A's determinant.'

'So A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone, and A⁻¹A = I, the do-nothing matrix.' puts two ideas and an appositive in one sentence; split it into 'So A then A⁻¹ leaves every point alone. That is A⁻¹A = I, the do-nothing matrix.'

findings.where: Screen 7 (Lean it flat), the plane at 360 px light and dark (moved state, j at 1.8)
findings.what: As j's tip nears (2, 1), j's ink arrow covers i's blue arrow almost completely, so the picture shows j 'leaning onto i's line' with no visible i; draw i's arrow above j's or thicken it so both stay visible.

findings.where: Screen 13 (Mixed: undo the grid), task and the '[6 2; 2 6] ÷ 40' answer
findings.what: The task already says the determinant is 32, so the '÷ 40' answer can be ruled out by rereading the question rather than by spotting the added-bc slip its hint explains; drop 'has determinant 32' from the task or replace that answer.

findings.where: Screen 10 (Solve it), the matrix label, hints, slip line and Why?
findings.what: The picture, hints and Why? call [2 1; 1 1] 'A' and its inverse 'A⁻¹' although screens 1 to 9 fix A = [3 1; 4 2], and the task never says the name has moved to a new matrix; call it B or say 'Here A = [2 1; 1 1]'.
The hint gives only the product's first entry (−13) and never names the slip it catches, reading the −1 as a minus sign; add 'The −1 means undo, not minus.'

findings.where: Screen 5 (The recipe), third worked row, and explain paragraph 3
findings.what: The general row '[d −b; −c a] × [a b; c d] = (ad − bc) × I' is stated, not shown; work one diagonal entry (d × a + (−b) × c = ad − bc) and one off-diagonal entry (d × b + (−b) × d = 0) so the rule is proved for every matrix, not only for A.

findings.where: Screen 9 (Equations as a move) and the finish line
findings.what: The finish says 'It turns AX = B into X = A⁻¹B', but no screen writes the equations as AX = B or shows A⁻¹ going on the left; screen 9's working rows could name X = (x, y) and B = (4, 6) and write X = A⁻¹B before the two row sums.

The brief's link to what he already knows is missing: with determinant 0 the two equations' lines are parallel or the same, as in Linear systems lesson 1; the lesson says only 'either no answer or many'.
The brief's point that a matrix that is not square has no inverse is never made; one sentence after 'It is called singular' would cover it.
The brief asked for the word 'symmetric' to be named once for the mirror pattern; the paragraph describes the pattern but never gives the name he will meet.

The matrix is only ever called the 'resistance grid' while 'grid' on the same screens also means the squared paper, and the name 'resistance matrix' he will meet in mesh-analysis texts never appears; name it once ('the resistance matrix, or grid').

'You cannot unsquish a line back into a plane.[^1]' is the source's own wording, footnoted although it is not a rule or value he would look up; say it in plain words of the lesson's own, e.g. 'Nothing can spread one line back out into a whole plane', and drop the footnote.

The breaks covers only the transformer half; the clamp half turns two currents into one number, whereas a singular 2 by 2 still gives two numbers tied to one line, and one sentence saying so would keep the comparison fully honest.

'The move A = [3 1; 4 2] sends i to (3, 4) and j to (1, 2), and the flag leans with the grid.' joins two ideas in about 20 words; end the sentence after (1, 2) and make 'The flag leans with the grid.' its own sentence.
'Round loop 1, 4I₁ + 2(I₁ − I₂) = 12, and round loop 2, 4I₂ + 2(I₂ − I₁) = 4.' carries two equations in one sentence; give each loop its own sentence.

'Swap a and d, which are both 6, and change the signs of b and c to get [6 2; 2 6].' has an aside in the middle; write 'a and d are both 6, so swapping them changes nothing. Change the signs of b and c to get [6 2; 2 6].'

findings.where: Screen 7 (Lean it flat), the only control
findings.what: The brief's interactive let him drag both columns of A against a live target; the build gives one slider that moves j's tip from 1 to 2 on a single screen, and every other screen is played to him or picked from three answers. It still shows the cause well, but a freer drag on screen 3 or 9 would give him more to play with.
